sections.title: AI before you open a chat

blocks.text: You take a photo of a friend and the camera draws a box around their face. Later, a streaming service suggests another episode for you. You may be using AI in both cases, with no chat window in sight. In the first case the system looks for a face in a picture. In the second it picks something you might enjoy. (1)

AI is short for **artificial intelligence**. In this book, we use that name for a family of computer systems that take information and use it to produce a result for a task. A result might be a prediction, a suggestion, a decision or something it creates, such as text or a picture. (1)

sections.title: What goes in and what comes out?

blocks.text: Imagine an app that recognises birds. You record a bird singing outside your window. The recording is the **input**, or what the system gets. The app suggests ‘blackbird’. That’s the **output**, or what the system gives back. If two birds were singing at once, the suggestion could be wrong. (1)

Thinking about what goes in and what comes out can help you see what a system does. An email filter gets a message and decides whether it should go into the spam folder. A translation app gets a sentence from you and gives you a translation. Both work with information, and each gives a different kind of result because it was built for a different job. (1)

sections.title: A rule or a set of examples?

blocks.text: You want to filter out suspicious messages. You could write a rule that says ‘Flag every message with the word “won” in it.’ You soon notice that an email from a friend congratulating you on winning a race goes into the spam folder too. So you add another rule. And then another.

**Machine learning** takes a different approach. People put together examples of messages and mark which ones are spam. A program adjusts a model so it gets better at telling which is which. The model can pick up on several clues at once, though it can still get things wrong. Rules and learning from data can both be part of the same system. (1, 2)

sections.title: What does it mean for a model to learn?

blocks.text: We want to build a model that can tell apples from pears in photos. We show it lots of photos and give it the right name for each fruit. That collection of examples is a **dataset**. The name attached to each photo is a **label**. As the model learns, the program changes numbers inside it so it gives the right name more often. (2)

This is one way to do machine learning. It’s called **supervised learning** because the dataset contains examples with the right answers. There are also ways for a program to look for patterns without using labels. For example, it might group similar photos together before anyone names the groups. (2)

sections.title: An apple the model has never seen

blocks.text: In our example dataset, all the apples are on white plates and the pears are on blue ones. The model recognises the fruit in those photos very well. Then you take an apple off its plate and the model starts to get confused. It may have picked up on the colour behind the fruit as a stronger clue than what the fruit itself looks like. (2)

We want the model to do well on new examples of the same kind. This ability is called **generalisation**. In our case, we could collect photos of different fruits against lots of backgrounds and test the model on pictures it hasn’t seen in training. A high score on pictures it already knows tells us little about how it’ll do in that test. (2)

sections.title: The model and the app have different jobs

blocks.text: Back to the birds outside your window. The **model** processes the recording and suggests the kind of bird it might be. The **app** gives you a button to record, shows you the result and sometimes lets you save what you found. One app can use several models. The same model can also help power several different apps. (1, 3)

In a chat, the message history and the box you type in are parts of the app. A language model usually writes the reply. The app can also get information from a file you’ve attached or from a search engine. That’s worth remembering when someone says ‘the AI saved something’ or ‘the AI looked at a website’. In both cases, what it can do may depend on the features of the app. (3)

A model for recognising bird calls can be excellent at its job. A conversation in French is a different job entirely. Some systems are built for narrow tasks like recognising birds. Others can be used for many different jobs. A language model, for example, can draft messages, summarise pieces of writing and help with translation. (1, 3)

A list of features only tells you so much about how well a model will do in a particular situation. Even a very good translation tool can get a place name wrong or miss the meaning of an unusual saying. When you’re choosing a tool, it helps to ask ‘Can it do my task on an example where I can check the result?’

A program that draws a box around a bird in a photo recognises something that’s already there. If you say ‘Draw a blackbird riding a bicycle’, an image generator can make a picture from your description. Creating things is what gives **generative AI** its name. These systems can make text, images, audio or video. What they can do depends on the model and the app. (1, 4)

A generated picture can look like a real photograph. How it looks tells you very little about whether the scene ever took place. A blackbird riding a bicycle is easy to take as a joke. For a more everyday scene, it’s worth finding out where the image came from before you treat it as evidence.

sections.title: When AI gets a photo and a question

blocks.text: You take a photo of a cardboard rocket and write ‘How could I improve this design?’ We call a model **multimodal** if it can use different kinds of information together, like the picture and the words in this example. ‘Modality’ here means a kind of information. Images, text and sound are different modalities. (4)

Multimodality tells you what kinds of information a model can work with. Generation tells you whether it can create something. A model can be both multimodal and generative. For example, it might take a photo and a question, then write an answer. Another system might use a picture just to recognise an object and tell you its name. (1, 4)

sections.title: What’s on the other side of the screen?

blocks.text: You tap the screen and ask an app for a dinner idea. A moment later, an answer appears. The screen only shows the last step. Somewhere along the way, a computer had to do some calculations. Sometimes that happens on the device in your hand. Sometimes it happens on a computer connected to it over the internet.

A model needs hardware and software to work. Hardware means the physical parts you can see and touch, like the electronic chips in your phone. Software tells the hardware what to do. In this chapter, we’ll look at the parts you could hold in your hand and what they need to work. (1, 2)

Silicon is an element, one of the basic building blocks of matter. In nature, it often occurs joined to oxygen. Together, they form silicon dioxide, also called silica. Quartz, a mineral found in sand, is one form of silica.

Quartz of the right quality can be used to make silicon. It needs to be processed and purified several times to make it suitable for electronics. Very pure silicon can be grown into a large crystal. The crystal is then cut into thin, round slices and carefully polished. Each slice is called a **silicon wafer**. Many chips can be made on a single wafer. (3, 4)

sections.title: A switch too small to see

blocks.text: An electronic chip contains many tiny parts called **transistors**. Think of a transistor as a switch. You move a light switch by hand. In a transistor, an electrical signal controls the flow of electricity. By connecting switches, engineers can build circuits that do calculations.

Silicon is called a semiconductor. Its ability to carry electricity can be changed. Engineers can do this in selected areas of a wafer by adding a tiny amount of another element, such as boron or phosphorus. This is called **doping**. It lets engineers give each area the properties it needs for a particular part to work. (4, 5)

sections.title: How light helps make a chip

blocks.text: When you take a photo, light forms an image on the camera’s sensor. In a chip factory, light transfers a pattern onto a wafer coated with a layer that reacts to light. This is called **photolithography**. The pattern shows where to keep material and where to remove it in later steps.

The factory repeats similar steps for many layers, which have to line up exactly. Some layers keep parts apart, while others connect them. Copper is one of the materials used for these connections. Finally, the chips are separated from the wafer, tested and placed in protective cases so they can be fitted and connected to the rest of the device. (5, 6)

A computer needs a **CPU**, its main processor. It follows instructions from programs and handles many different kinds of tasks. The **GPU** was designed with graphics in mind. When making an image, there are lots of similar calculations that can happen at the same time. That ability also comes in handy when a neural network has many calculations to do at once.

Some chips are designed to speed up particular kinds of calculations. They are called **accelerators** because they help get the work done faster. A GPU can work as an accelerator. Another example is the TPU, designed by Google for machine learning calculations. A computer can use several kinds of processors. (7, 8)

sections.title: Where a computer keeps its numbers

blocks.text: When you’re working on a problem, you might keep your notebook open on your desk and leave the books you need on a shelf. A computer also needs room for what it is using right now and a place to keep files for later.

A file containing a trained model can be kept in storage, on an SSD for example. While it is running, the computer uses working memory. The chip doing the calculations needs to get the right numbers quickly. With some large models, it could spend a lot of time just waiting for those numbers to arrive. That’s why some accelerators use fast memory such as **HBM**, which is designed to move lots of data in a short time. (1, 9)

A server is a computer that does jobs for other devices. You can send it a photo to process or ask it to answer a question. In a data centre, servers sit in racks connected by cables and networking equipment. The building also contains equipment for storing data, supplying power and keeping the machines cool.

When someone says an app runs ‘in the cloud’, they may mean it uses a provider’s computers and services over the internet. The people who make the app can rent the computing power they need. The user just sees the app working. The same equipment can also run ordinary websites, email and video services. (1, 10)

sections.title: What a phone can do on its own

blocks.text: Some AI tasks can run on the device itself. For example, an app might use a model on your phone to tidy up a short note. That model needs to fit the phone’s available memory, processing power and battery capacity. If everything the feature needs is already on the device, it can do the calculations without an internet connection.

An app from the same company might send other tasks to servers. Where the calculation happens depends on the feature and the settings. If you want to know what data leaves your device, check the description of the feature you’re using. The word ‘AI’ on the screen gives you very little information about that. (2)

A laptop gets warm when it works hard for a long time. In a data centre, the same thing happens in many computers at once. The equipment needs electricity to do its calculations. The heat has to be carried away to keep the machines at the right temperature.

Air and circulating liquids are two ways to cool the equipment. The method depends on the machines, the building and local conditions. In some cooling systems, water evaporates and carries heat away. Others use air in place of water at one stage of the process. The size of a building alone tells you very little about how much water it uses. (1, 11)

sections.title: What does it take to answer one question?

blocks.text: It’s hard to answer with a single number. Writing a short reply and generating an image take different kinds of work. It also matters which model does the job, what equipment it runs on and how long the reply is. If you’re asking about water, check what was measured. It might cover the water used to cool the building, the water used to generate the electricity, or both.

If you see a figure for a data centre’s electricity use, check what it covers. A data centre can run many services, and only some of its work may involve AI. A measurement from one site or one task tells you about that particular case. (1, 12, 14, 15)

sections.title: What happens to the equipment afterwards

blocks.text: Making a device starts with obtaining and preparing raw materials. The parts have to be made and assembled. Then the equipment has to be transported and supplied with electricity when it runs. When a chip can no longer handle the hardest calculations, the computer it’s in may still be able to do another job. Worn-out equipment can be taken to a suitable collection point for further processing.

Each of these stages matters when we talk about AI’s impact on the environment. The electricity meter where a server runs shows just one part of the story. It’s also worth asking how long the equipment will be used and what will happen to its parts afterwards. (3, 12, 13)

blocks.text: When you recognise an apple, you might notice its shape, its colour and its stalk. A model works with numbers. For example, a photo can be stored as numbers that describe the colours of its tiny dots, called pixels. In a **neural network**, each set of calculations passes its results on to the next until the network produces an answer. (1)

The way these calculations are connected is called the model’s **architecture**. As it works, the network also uses a huge number of values called **parameters**. You can think of them as settings that affect the result. In a simple model, changing one value might give one clue more weight. In a large network, many values work together, and their effects are hard to explain with a list of simple rules. (1)

sections.title: Where does the training material come from?

blocks.text: That depends on the task. A model that recognises birds by their calls needs recordings. A language model can learn from books, articles and other collections of text. The people building it choose sources and prepare the data. They might remove duplicates, filter out poor-quality material and add examples in languages the system will need to handle later. (2, 3)

People can make material especially for training. It can also come from public sources or be shared under agreements. The choice of material raises questions about permission and the rights of the people who created it. To find out what went into a particular model, look for an explanation from its makers. They might describe the kinds of material they used without listing every text. (2, 3)

Imagine the sentence ‘After the rain, there was a huge … on the pavement.’ One word that fits is ‘puddle’. During training, the model sees the start of a sentence, and the program compares its prediction with the next part of the original. If the model gave the correct word a very low chance, the program changes some of its parameters to help it do better on this kind of task. (1, 4)

The program repeats this exercise with a huge number of examples. The model starts to pick up patterns. It learns which pieces of words often appear next to each other, how sentences fit together and how earlier text can change what a sentence means. In training, the program can look up the next part in the data. In a real conversation, there may be no known right answer. (4, 5)

When you do practice questions with an answer sheet, you can check your work. If you later take a test made up of the very same questions, your score tells you little about how you would handle a new one. It’s similar for a model. Its makers can test it on examples they kept out of training. (6)

Think again about recognising birds. A model does well with clear recordings from the woods, but it sometimes mixes up species when there’s traffic in the background. If you want it to help in towns too, include those conditions in the test. A test result tells you how the model did under those particular conditions. To see how it performs somewhere different, you’ll need to try it there too. (6)

sections.title: From finishing sentences to having a conversation

blocks.text: After its first round of training, a language model may be able to finish a sentence. Ask it for three ideas for a school trip, though, and it might carry on writing as if your question were the start of an article. To help it follow instructions, its makers can give it **more training**. They might show it a request and an example of a good answer. In other exercises, people compare several answers and choose the one that best meets their expectations. (7)

A model can also be fine-tuned for a particular job, such as taking notes in a set format. After making changes, it’s worth testing how they help in practice. Writing clear notes and getting the facts right are two separate skills. (3, 7)

sections.title: What happens when you send a question?

blocks.text: An ordinary chat uses a model that someone has already trained. You send a question, the app passes it to the model, and the model works out an answer. This stage is called **inference**. In a bird app, it could mean identifying the bird in a new recording. In a chat, it could mean writing a few sentences. (1, 4, 8)

If you write ‘I meant a blackbird, not a starling’ in the same chat, the next answer can take that correction into account because the app has passed on new information. That can happen without any change to the model’s parameters. The service’s own rules determine whether it might use the conversation later to improve its models. (3, 8, 9)

sections.title: What does a sentence look like to a model?

blocks.text: We can look at a sentence and see individual words. Before a language model can do calculations with text, a program breaks it into small units called **tokens**. A token can be a whole word, part of a word, a punctuation mark or another piece of text. The split depends on the program and the language, so two models might break up the same sentence differently. (4)

Each piece gets a number from the model’s vocabulary. The calculations start with those numbers. Tokens are worth knowing about as a user too. The amount of a conversation the model can consider at once is often measured in tokens. A long file and a short paragraph take up different amounts of that space. (4, 5)

sections.title: How does a model know what we’re talking about?

blocks.text: If someone writes ‘Put it next to the bank’, the word ‘bank’ might make you think of a building or a business. If you’ve just been discussing a game with a points bank, the same word could refer to a part of the game. The **context**, or the information that goes with the sentence, helps you work out what it means. (4)

For a model, the context might include your question, earlier messages and part of a document supplied by the app. There’s a limit to how much information the model can consider at once. That limit is called the **context window**. If a conversation gets too long to fit, older details can drop out of the context. Sometimes all you need to do is repeat an important sentence in a new message. (4, 5, 9)

sections.title: The answer comes together one piece at a time

blocks.text: Try sending this request. ‘Write two sentences about rain for a younger reader.’ Many language models build the answer by weighing up which token could come next. One version might start ‘From the clouds …’. Another might start ‘When …’. Once the model has chosen a piece, it takes that piece into account as it chooses the next one. That’s how it builds up the text. (4, 8)

The settings for how the model makes each choice can affect how much the answer varies when you repeat a request. One answer might say ‘Rain falls from clouds when drops of water get big enough.’ Another might compare the drops to tiny balls. The model’s training helps it carry an idea through several sentences. (4, 8)

To create a picture, some models start with something like the speckled static on an old television. As they make changes step by step, shapes and details begin to emerge. This is one way of generating an image. Models that work this way are called **diffusion models**. (10)

When you can guide the model with text, your description helps shape the result. Ask for ‘a red umbrella at an empty bus stop in the rain’ and the model tries to make a picture that fits. Changing ‘red’ to ‘yellow’ could change the umbrella and other parts of the scene. Take a look at the result. The model can add a detail you never asked for or leave out one you wanted. (11)

sections.title: Does a chatbot always search the internet?

blocks.text: You ask what time the library closes. The model can put a time in a sentence that sounds perfectly natural. You’ll still need to check the library’s current opening hours. If the app has a search tool and uses it, it can give the model part of the library’s website so the answer can draw on that information. A document you add can supply text to discuss in the same way. (12, 13)

A chat app might also have a tool for maths. Depending on the app, the tool can do a calculation and return the result to the chat. These are separate features that can help the model answer. If you need opening hours, open the page the app points you to and check that the time is for the right library and the right day. (13)

sections.title: What does it mean when a chatbot remembers something?

blocks.text: In one chat you might write ‘Please explain things without technical terms’ and later ask for a description of a film. If your earlier request is still in the context, the model can use it when it replies. A new chat might have a different set of information available. (4, 9)

Some apps have a **memory** feature. It can pass information from earlier chats into new ones, such as your preference for short explanations. This depends on the app and its settings. The patterns picked up during training are a separate matter. Information in the model’s parameters works differently from a library where you can open any document. A model can sometimes repeat passages from its training material word for word. (9, 14)

sections.title: A smooth answer can still be wrong

blocks.text: Imagine asking a chatbot for the title of a book you heard about on the radio. It gives you a plausible author’s name, publication year and publisher. The whole thing looks like an entry in a library catalogue. When you look for the book in the catalogue, it turns out that the model made up a convincing description. Made-up details like these are sometimes called **AI hallucinations**. (15)

A smooth style tells you the answer is well written. You can check whether it’s true separately. If an answer depends on a particular number, promise or name, look for it in the original source. Start by asking how we know. That habit will help when you try out prompts for yourself later in the book. (13, 15)

chapters.title: The people and companies behind AI

sections.title: How many people does it take to get one answer?

blocks.text: Think about the button you tap to send a question in an AI chat. Someone decided where the button would go and how it would work. Other people prepared the model that helps write the answer. Other teams designed the chips, set up the servers and make sure they’re available when you need them.

Companies and teams do different jobs. One organisation sometimes has several roles. To understand what it does, ask which part of the work it takes on. You’ll meet some examples in this chapter. The names and roles were checked on 20 November 2026. (1)

sections.title: Who draws up a plan for a chip?

blocks.text: Before a chip can be made, engineers decide what parts it needs and how they will connect. Think of the floor plan of a flat. It shows where the walls, doors and plug sockets will go. Engineers have to arrange the parts of a chip so information can flow between them and the chip does the job it’s supposed to do.

NVIDIA and AMD are examples of companies that design chips used in AI and other fields. Specialised factories make the wafers that hold their chips. Companies that design hardware can also make software to help programmers use those chips. (2, 3)

The design is only the first step. You need a factory that can turn it into a real chip. One company that offers this service is **TSMC**, which started in Taiwan. It makes chips based on its customers’ designs. **Samsung** and **Intel** also manufacture semiconductors and design chips of their own.

A factory has to repeat many of the steps in the chapter on hardware with great care and precision. It also needs to test which chips work properly. That’s why the name on a finished graphics card might be the name of the company that designed its chip, even when another company made the chip itself. (4, 5, 6, 7)

sections.title: Who builds the machines for the factories?

blocks.text: In a chip factory, each machine has a job. One adds a thin layer of material. Another helps make a pattern on it. A third checks whether the pattern is exactly where it should be.

**ASML**, a company from the Netherlands, makes photolithography machines, among other things. These machines use light to transfer patterns onto a wafer. A toolmaker can play a big part in making new chips, even if you’re unlikely to see its name on a list of what’s in your phone. The companies that supply wafers, materials, parts and measuring equipment also help make each chip possible. (7, 8)

Imagine a small team wants to launch an app that can recognise what’s in a photo. The app might have a hundred users one day and a thousand the next. Renting computing power over the internet from a cloud provider saves the team the work of buying and setting up more computers.

**Amazon Web Services**, **Microsoft Azure** and **Google Cloud** are examples of providers. They offer different kinds of hardware and tools for training or running models. Google is an example of an organisation that does several jobs. It offers cloud services and designs its own accelerators, while teams at Google DeepMind build the Gemini models. (9, 10, 11, 12)

sections.title: Who makes the models and chat apps?

blocks.text: **OpenAI** builds models and provides the ChatGPT app. **Google DeepMind** develops Gemini models. **Anthropic** makes the family of models called Claude, and **Meta** develops the Llama family. You may see these organisations in the news about AI. **Mistral AI** and **DeepSeek** are two more examples of teams that develop models. (12–17)

When you use an AI chat, you see a window for your conversation and some buttons. That’s the app. The model does some of the work inside it, such as helping write replies. An app may let you choose a model. The same model can also work inside different apps. That helps explain why two services that look different may be able to do similar things. (12, 13, 14)

During training, the numbers that affect how a model works change. Many of these numbers are called **weights**. Sometimes the people who build a model let you download its weights, along with information about how to run it. If you have the right hardware and software, you can use the model on your own computer. Some models in the Llama and gpt-oss families are examples of models with weights you can download. (15, 18)

Downloading the weights gives you a part you need to run the model. For details about whether the training data and code are available, or what you’re allowed to do with the model, look for separate information. Two releases described as ‘open’ may let you do different things. (19)

sections.title: Who chooses the examples and checks the answers?

blocks.text: Imagine a team wants to build a model that helps people recognise plants. It needs photos and people to check their labels. If a label is wrong, the computer can end up learning from a bad example. When working on large language models, people may also write sample replies and judge which of several answers best follows the instructions.

Engineers, people who work with data and people who know the subject each bring different skills. Together they can spot mistakes a programmer working alone might miss. People’s feedback helps improve a model. Its answers still need testing. (1, 20)

How you check the result depends a lot on what the tool needs to do. Someone who studies plants could help test an app that recognises them. A teacher’s opinion matters when you’re checking a tool for learning to read. Testers can compare answers with trusted data, look for mistakes and see what happens when someone types in something unusual.

Universities and research institutions also work on AI. NASA is working with teams from companies and universities on a model that can help researchers study the Moon’s surface. It’s an example of a project that draws on computing methods and on the knowledge of people who have spent years studying data from space missions. (1, 21)

sections.title: How can you tell who did what?

blocks.text: When you read that a company ‘makes AI’, try to find out exactly what it did. Did it design the chip? Make it? Provide computers? Train the model? Put it into the app you use? Sometimes several of these answers are true.

Think back to the button you tapped to send a question. You now know how many steps might come before an answer appears. Each step brings a different question you can ask. You might ask the people who make the app what happens to your chat messages. You might ask the model researchers how they tested it for mistakes. It’s easier to look for a good answer when you know who to ask. (1)

sections.title: A video you can watch without sound

blocks.text: Imagine a friend has sent you a video. You’re on the bus, your headphones are at home, and you want to know what she’s saying. Captions can appear on the screen as the video plays.

In 2019, Google showed how Live Caption worked directly on its Pixel 4 phone, even without an internet connection. One model recognised speech, another added punctuation, and a third recognised certain sounds. (1)

Deaf and hard-of-hearing people helped develop the feature. For them, captions make it possible to follow videos that would otherwise be difficult to access. On the bus, you might simply find the same feature handy. (2)

Early in the morning, a short whistle comes from the bushes. The leaves hide the bird, but you can record its call. BirdNET, a project run by teams at Cornell University and Chemnitz University of Technology, uses machine learning to recognise birds by sound. (3)

If you’re out on a walk, the suggested species can give you something to look up in a bird guide. For people who study wildlife, a tool like this can help sift through large sets of recordings and pick out clips to check more closely. That helps when you can hear several birds, the wind and sometimes passing cars in the same place. Listening can reveal the presence of an animal that nobody can see at the time. (3)

sections.title: A planet hidden in the readings

blocks.text: When a planet passes in front of its star as seen through a telescope, it blocks some of the star’s light. Imagine moving a small ball in front of a lamp. At a distance you might struggle to see the ball itself, but a sensitive instrument could notice the light dim slightly for a moment.

In 2017, researchers used a model trained on examples to look for signs like these in older readings from the Kepler space telescope. That’s how they found a signal from the planet Kepler-90i. The planet takes about 14 days to go round its star. Imagine having a year that short. Among thousands of readings, machine learning helped pick out a faint signal that was easy to miss. (4)

sections.title: Two ways to forecast the weather

blocks.text: How does a forecast work out where a storm might go? A traditional weather model uses the laws of physics to calculate what might happen next in the atmosphere. A machine-learning model uses earlier data to learn how conditions in the atmosphere change over time.
In February 2025, the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts started using its AI system, called AIFS, for regular forecasts. The forecasting teams could use results from both models. (5)

Think about a forecast for the day of a trip. If the predicted time for rain shifts as the day gets closer, it makes sense to check again. A forecast is based on what we can observe and calculate at the time.

sections.title: A scroll best left rolled up

blocks.text: In AD 79, Mount Vesuvius erupted, burying Herculaneum and charring its papyrus scrolls. Some are so brittle that trying to unroll them could badly damage them. Researchers used X-rays to see inside and computer programs to view the layers of the scroll on a screen. (6)

Machine learning helped a team in the Vesuvius Challenge recognise traces of ink. Experts in ancient writing checked which parts could be read. The competition results came out in 2024. The sections the team could read were about 2,000 years old and discussed pleasures such as music and food. It’s a detail that lets us see the ancient writers as people with interests we recognise today. (6)

sections.title: The missing edges of a Rembrandt painting

blocks.text: Imagine a family photo with its edges cut off. Luckily, an old copy of the whole picture still exists, though its colours are slightly different. You can see who was standing at the side and try to recreate what the missing part looked like.

The Rijksmuseum faced a similar problem with Rembrandt’s *The Night Watch*. Part of the canvas was cut away in the 18th century. The museum team used a 17th-century copy and neural networks to recreate the missing parts in the style of the painting. In 2021, it showed the reconstruction alongside the surviving canvas. (7)
The copy helped the team work out what had been at the edges. The reconstructed pieces showed visitors what the whole picture might have looked like.

sections.title: What does a protein look like?

blocks.text: Proteins are molecules that do a great deal of work inside living things. One of them, haemoglobin, helps red blood cells carry oxygen. (8) The shape of a molecule is one of the clues scientists use to understand how it works.

AlphaFold can predict the shapes of many proteins. In 2022, DeepMind and EMBL’s European Bioinformatics Institute released an update to their shared database with more than 200 million of these predictions. (9)

It’s a bit like looking at a model of a building before going inside. The model helps you decide where to look. Scientists who want to answer a precise question about a protein’s shape or what it does may still need measurements and experiments.

sections.title: When a player surprised the program

blocks.text: In 2016, Lee Sedol, one of the world’s best Go players, played five games against AlphaGo. In Go, players place black and white stones on a board and try to surround territory. In the second game, the program surprised people watching with its 37th move. It chose a place on the board that experienced players were unlikely to expect. (10)

In the fourth game, the surprise came from the other side. Lee Sedol made an unusual move, number 78, and won that game. AlphaGo won the match four games to one, and players studied both sides’ moves afterwards. (10) The next time you play a board game, ask yourself whether there’s a spot on the board you haven’t even considered.

blocks.text: Start with a simple question. ‘Why do leaves change colour?’ is already a **prompt**. A prompt is what you type when you ask AI a question or tell it what you’d like help with. The words you’d use in an everyday conversation will do.

If the answer is too difficult, say what sort of answer you need. ‘Explain it to someone who has never heard of chlorophyll. Give one example from a park and use no more than three sentences.’ Now you’ve said who the answer is for, how long it should be and where to find an example. If ‘chlorophyll’ still sounds unfamiliar, ask what that word means. Your second question can be shorter than your first. (1)

sections.title: Say what you want to get back

blocks.text: ‘Help me with my presentation’ could mean asking for an idea, planning slides or practising a talk. You can specify the length and the subject, as in this prompt.

Plan a five-minute presentation about what bees do in a garden. My audience knows bees mostly from pictures and walks outdoors. Suggest an opening, three main points and a question for the audience. Leave room for an example of my own.

You’ll get an outline to which you can add your own photo or story. The same approach works when you’re writing a message. You can ask for two sentences, a calm tone or a version for someone who is hearing about the issue for the first time. (1)

sections.title: Include details that change the answer

blocks.text: Imagine asking for a dinner idea. The number of people, your four ingredients and the fact that you only have a frying pan all change the answer. Your address, surname and phone number add nothing to that task.

When you write to a company, you can paste just the part of their reply that needs explaining. Remove names, addresses and order numbers. In the draft, replace them with words in brackets, then fill in the real details yourself before you send it. If you need help with something that concerns another person, a description in your own words is usually enough. (2)

sections.title: Improve the answer a bit at a time

blocks.text: You ask for a short message to a neighbour and get a letter that sounds as if it came from a council office. Try adding ‘The first sentence is good. Shorten the rest and use words I’d say if I bumped into my neighbour on the stairs.’ This shows which part to keep and what to change. (1)

If the chat misses an important detail, spell it out. For dinner, you might say ‘I’ve only got ten minutes left.’ For a translation, try ‘This is a message to a friend. Keep it relaxed.’ You can start a new chat when you change the subject so the earlier instructions don’t get mixed up with the next task.

sections.title: Check before you use the answer

blocks.text: Suppose the draft of your presentation includes a claim like this. ‘Bees visit ten thousand flowers a day.’ It sounds precise. Before you repeat that figure, find out what it describes. One bee? A whole colony? Perhaps one species in particular conditions?

Ask for the title of the source and a link. Open the link and check whether the author really gave that information. If you’re drafting a message, compare it with the facts you know. When the answer could affect someone’s health, money or safety, base your decision on a reliable source and ask someone qualified to help if you need to. (2)

Pick a task where you’ll be able to tell whether the answer helped. Ask AI to simplify three sentences from a set of instructions, then compare the two versions. If you’re learning a language, try acting out a short conversation in a café and write down one phrase you’ll use the next time.

If you’d like to understand more of the theory, **Elements of AI** offers an introduction that doesn’t require programming. If you’re more curious about how to build something yourself, the same project offers **Building AI**. Start with a subject you’re curious enough about to think of a second question once you’ve read the first answer. (3)

intro.text: Start with a task you actually have to do. Copy the prompt and replace the words in square brackets with your own details. If there’s something you don’t know yet, say so. Under each prompt there’s a follow-up you can try to see how the answer changes when you add one more detail.

sections.title: 1. A firm message to customer service

blocks.text: Use this prompt if a company has turned down a complaint or given you an unclear reply. Say what you’d like them to do next.

Help me write to customer service. [Describe what happened.] The company replied [summarise their reply without personal details]. I’d like to ask for [what you want them to do]. Suggest a subject line and a short, polite but firm message. Stick to the facts I gave you. Ask me about any important information that’s missing.
**Try this next.** ‘Make the message shorter and keep one clear request.’
Start with what you have to hand. Use the rice, eggs, carrots and peas from the beginning of the book, or put in your own ingredients.

I have [four ingredients and roughly how much of each] as well as [basics I have, such as water, salt and oil]. I’m cooking for [number of people], I have [time available] and I can use [equipment]. Allow for [dietary requirements, or write ‘none’]. Suggest a meal with these ingredients. Give the quantities, the steps in order and roughly how long it will take. If you need to add an ingredient, ask me first.
**Try this next.** ‘I only have one frying pan. How should I change the order of the steps?’
Try this when you know what you’re trying to do but the instructions are hard to follow. Keep the original handy so you can compare it with the answer.

Help me understand this part of the instructions. [Paste the part you need.] Explain in plain language what the step is for. Put the actions in the order I should do them and explain any difficult words I need to know. Keep the warnings from the original. Point out anything that is unclear or can’t be explained from the part I shared.
**Try this next.** ‘Explain step [number] in more detail. According to the instructions, how can I tell if I’ve done it correctly?’
You’d write differently to a friend than you would to a school or a hotel. Tell the chat who will read your message.

Translate this message into [language]. Here’s the message [paste it here]. I’m writing to [say who will read it]. Give me two versions, one more formal and one more casual. Keep the meaning and all the facts. If a sentence could mean two different things, ask me what I mean.
**Try this next.** ‘Translate the second version back into [the language I wrote it in] so I can check the meaning.’
Enter when your classes or meetings are and what you’re trying to fit in between them.

Help me plan my day from [start time] to [end time]. My fixed plans are [list with times]. I need to do [list with a rough time for each task]. The most important tasks are [your priorities]. Include breaks, meals and time between activities. If there isn’t room for everything, show me what I could move to another day.
**Try this next.** ‘I have one hour less. Change the plan so I can still do the two most important things.’

sections.title: 6. Practising a conversation in another language

blocks.text: Choose a situation you might find yourself in. For your first try, you could order something in a café.

Help me practise a conversation in [language] in this situation [for example, ordering something in a café]. My level is [for example, beginner]. Play the other person. Write one short line at a time and wait for my reply. When I make a mistake, show me a more natural way to say it, then carry on with the conversation. You go first.
**Try this next.** ‘Let’s end the conversation. Pick three phrases we used and explain when to use them.’
You can compare two ways to spend an afternoon or two ways of doing the same task. Say what matters to you.

Help me compare [option A] and [option B]. Here are the facts I have [add the details]. What matters most to me is [what you care about]. Make a simple table of the advantages, disadvantages and things I’d need to check. Mark any missing facts as unknown. Explain how my top priority affects the choice.
**Try this next.** ‘What if convenience matters most to me now and speed comes second?’

sections.title: 8. A packing list for a trip

blocks.text: Include how long you’ll be away and how much space you have in your bag. That can change the list more than the name of your destination.

Help me pack for [number of days]. I’m going [for example, to the mountains, to see family or to a city], travelling by [transport], staying [type of accommodation] and taking [type of bag]. I plan to [activities]. Here’s what I know about the conditions [for example, it might rain]. Split the list into essentials and extras. Point out anything I should check separately if I haven’t given you enough information.
**Try this next.** ‘I only have one small backpack. Given my plans, what could I most easily leave behind?’
Try this if you want to explain something calmly, ask for a change or say no. Describe the situation without using names.

Help me prepare for a conversation about [subject]. Here’s what happened. [Describe the situation briefly.] I want to say [what matters to you] and I hope to [your goal]. Ask me two questions about the situation first. Once I answer, suggest a calm, natural way to start the conversation and two ways the other person might respond. Treat their reactions as examples I can practise with.
**Try this next.** ‘Act out one of those reactions and wait for me to reply.’
You can use this prompt as it is. The chat should give a brief reply and wait for your first question.

Let’s play 20 questions. Secretly choose one well-known person or character, an object or an animal. Keep the same choice for the whole game. Answer my questions only with ‘YES’, ‘NO’ or ‘I DON’T KNOW’. After my twentieth question, tell me the answer if I haven’t guessed. If I guess sooner, tell me I’ve won. For now, just say ‘Ready’ and wait.

**Try this next.** ‘Let’s swap roles. I’ll choose something and you ask me one question at a time.’ When you’re the one keeping the answer secret, you can see whether the chat’s questions really narrow down the options.

sections.title: Two answers can sound just as convincing

blocks.text: Imagine you’re going on a trip tomorrow. You ask a chatbot what time the bus leaves. The answer sounds certain. It gives you a time, the name of the stop and even the bus number. The next morning, you get to the stop and find out that the timetable changed two months ago.

That’s a small example of a bigger problem. AI can sound just as convincing when the information it gives you is true, out of date or completely made up. When a model presents something made up as fact, people often call it a ‘hallucination’. It might even make up a book title or a web address to back up its answer. (1)
If you’re looking for ideas for a game, a mistake like that might cost you very little. When you need the answer to make a decision, checking it is part of the job.

Start by asking which detail matters to your decision. For the bus, it’s the departure time. Look it up in the timetable on the bus company’s website. Make sure you’ve got the right day, direction and stop.

You can ask the AI where it got the information. Open the source it gives you and see whether it actually supports the answer. If the chatbot can’t get up-to-date information, find the part you need yourself, paste it into the chat and ask for help understanding it.

For questions about health or safety, use reliable sources and ask someone with the right knowledge. If the instructions for a device seem unclear, go back to the original manual. That’s a better place to start than another smooth-sounding answer. (1)

sections.title: What to keep out of the chat

blocks.text: You want AI to help improve a message about a missing parcel. All it needs is a description of what happened and what you want the company to do. You can put ‘address’, ‘phone number’ and ‘order number’ in place of your real home address, phone number and parcel details. Fill in the real details when you’re ready to send the finished message to the delivery company.

The same idea applies to photos and documents. Before you attach a file, look at the whole page or photo. There may be a signature in the corner of a document, or someone in the background of a photo who hasn’t agreed to have it shared. With an online chatbot, how your information is stored and used depends on the service and its settings. If a short summary without personal details will do, use that. (1)

sections.title: Who does the same program work for?

blocks.text: Imagine a school is testing a program that turns speech into text. It gets almost everything right in the trial. Only when the teacher looks at each person’s results separately does she notice that the program often gets the words wrong for a few people. The average score hides that pattern.

The *Gender Shades* project measured a similar difference. In 2018, researchers Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru tested three programs that used photos of people to sort them into one of two gender categories. In that particular test, the systems made far more mistakes in photos of women with darker skin than in photos of men with lighter skin. (2)
When you’re judging a system, ask who it makes mistakes for and when those mistakes happen. This is especially important when a tool can affect someone’s work, education or access to services. (1)

Someone calls who sounds like your cousin. They’re speaking quickly and asking for help straight away. Hearing a familiar voice might make you believe them before you’ve had time to think. Scammers sometimes use a voice made by AI to pretend to be someone you know. (3)

If the caller asks for money or a code, or tells you to keep the call a secret, hang up. Call the person on a number you already know, or ask someone close to you to check what’s happening. If you’re a child, show the message to an adult you trust. (3)

Something similar can happen with images. A realistic video can show a person saying or doing something that never happened. Before you share a shocking clip, check who posted it and whether an independent, reliable source confirms what it shows. (1)

One job can involve many different tasks. Someone who runs a small shop takes deliveries, talks to customers and updates prices. AI could help write a product description. The owner still needs to check the final price, and sometimes a conversation is the best way to find out what a customer is asking for.

In 2025, researchers at the International Labour Organization estimated that generative AI could affect some of the tasks done by about one in four workers worldwide. The researchers expected changes to the way people work to be more likely than the loss of an entire occupation in most of the jobs that could be affected. They estimated what might happen to tasks. The number of jobs people actually lose also depends on what companies and others decide to do. (4)
It also matters who benefits from the time saved and who gets the help they need to learn new tasks.

sections.title: Who can put a decision right?

blocks.text: Imagine a program is helping to give out places at a school workshop. It reads one of the forms incorrectly. A pupil is told she hasn’t got a place, even though she signed up on time.

The person in charge should be able to look at the form and check the result against the sign-up rules. The pupil needs to know who to speak to about the mistake. That gives her a real chance to have the decision put right.

When an organisation starts using AI, it’s worth asking, ‘Who can spot a mistake, and what can they do about it?’ Testing the program first, giving people a way to report a problem and letting someone put it right all matter, even if the program usually works well. The people and organisations that choose the tool remain responsible for how they use it. (1)

Ask AI to draft an invitation and you’ll get some text. If the app can access your calendar and has permission, it can also add a meeting. On screen, the two requests look similar. The second one changes something outside the chat.

A system that can plan and carry out steps on its own using tools is often called an AI agent. What it can do depends in part on what it has been given access to. You can delete a draft that contains a mistake. It’s harder to take back a message sent to the wrong people. One useful limit would be to have the agent show you the message and who will receive it, then wait for your approval before sending. (5)

A more complicated task means more decisions along the way. You need to decide which steps the system can handle, which ones need your approval and how to stop the task if something goes differently from what you planned.

Imagine a game where your score depends only on how many coins you collect. You could get a high score by repeating the easiest move, even if the game’s designer wanted players to explore and solve puzzles. Something similar can happen with AI. The score used to reward the system may capture only part of what a person meant it to do. (5)

When we look further into the future, the question gets harder. Could very advanced systems act so widely and on their own that people couldn’t take back control? The *International AI Safety Report 2026* shows how much experts disagree about that possibility. It describes what research has found so far and what new abilities systems would need before this could happen. Experts still disagree about how likely it is and how much harm it could cause. (5)

sections.title: Joy Buolamwini and the face a program missed

blocks.text: On 22 May 2019, Joy Buolamwini, a researcher in facial analysis and the founder of the Algorithmic Justice League, submitted written testimony to the US House of Representatives. She described what happened when she tried a program that detects faces. (6)
‘… facial analysis software failing to detect my dark-skinned face until I put on a white mask.’ (6)

The mask helped in that one test. Buolamwini was warning about a wider problem. Teams that measure only how well a system works on average might miss the cases where some people are more affected by mistakes. Her testimony covered technology that analyses and recognises faces, including how it can be used in ways that affect people’s civil rights. (6)

sections.title: Stephen Hawking and an uncertain future

blocks.text: On 19 October 2016, physicist Stephen Hawking spoke at the opening of a research centre on the future of intelligence at the University of Cambridge. He talked about what powerful AI could make possible for humanity and the dangers it could bring. (7)
‘In short, the rise of powerful AI will be either the best, or the worst thing, ever to happen to humanity.’ (7)

Hawking then said that nobody yet knew which of those possibilities would come true. He chose strong words to show how much could be at stake and why the research mattered. Both halves of his sentence belong together. (7)

sections.title: Geoffrey Hinton and the question of control

blocks.text: On 10 December 2024, Geoffrey Hinton spoke at the Nobel Prize banquet in Stockholm. He was one of two people awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for work that helped develop machine learning with neural networks. Near the end of his speech, he talked about the possibility of systems becoming more intelligent than people. (8)
‘We have no idea whether we can stay in control.’ (8)

Hinton believes the risk could have lasting effects and that we need research into how to stay in control. In the sentence before this, he was talking about possible future systems far more advanced than today’s. That is the situation he had in mind when he spoke about the risk. (8)

sections.title: Yoshua Bengio and decisions that affect everyone

blocks.text: On 23 September 2026, Yoshua Bengio spoke to the United Nations Security Council. Bengio is a machine learning researcher and a co-chair of the UN’s Independent International Scientific Panel on AI. He raised three concerns. People could misuse AI, a small number of groups could gain a great deal of power, and people could lose control of AI. (9)
‘Decisions that affect us all should be made by us all.’ (9)

Bengio called for independent safety checks and for countries to work together. His concern goes beyond the computer and the company that runs it. Who gets to check how a system works? Who takes responsibility for what happens? Who was missing from the room when the decision was made? (9)

sections.title: Yuval Noah Harari and trust in words

blocks.text: On 28 April 2023, the historian Yuval Noah Harari, author of *Sapiens*, published an essay in *The Economist* about how AI might affect language and society. He pointed out that more and more writing can be produced automatically, and readers can find it hard to tell who is speaking to them. (10)
‘Democracy is a conversation, and conversations rely on language.’ (10)

Think of an online discussion where lots of similar comments make it look as if crowds of people support an idea. If the comments were generated automatically, seeing them tells you little about how many people really think that way. That’s one way to understand Harari’s concern. In a wider conversation about technology, it matters who you can trust. (10)

sections.title: Yann LeCun and the trouble with comparisons

blocks.text: In a conversation with Lex Fridman published on 7 March 2024, neural network researcher Yann LeCun questioned whether progress in AI can come down to crossing a single line on a scale of intelligence. He also said that some scenarios in which people suddenly lose control were based on mistaken assumptions. (11)
‘… intelligence is not a linear thing that you can measure with a scale or with a single number.’ (11)

A computer can beat someone at chess and still need separate sensors and software to move around a flat. If you ask which is smarter, you miss the differences between those tasks. When you’re thinking about risk, try asking a more specific question. What can the system do, and what has it actually been given access to?

sections.title: What we can take from these warnings

blocks.text: Buolamwini studied errors she could measure. Harari considered how AI might affect the way people talk to one another. Hinton and Bengio asked how people can stay in control, while LeCun wanted a clearer account of what future systems might be able to do. Hawking drew attention to how widely the possible outcomes could differ.

When you hear a serious warning, try to find out what it’s based on. Has someone measured a problem, observed it in one situation, or thought through something that could happen in the future? Scientists have good reason to study dangers that are rare but could cause great harm. You can still ask what the evidence shows and where the predictions begin. (5)
You can use the same approach when someone promises that AI will solve a difficult problem. Ask them to be just as specific.

Go back to one of the prompts in this book. It might have been about dinner, a translation or a message about a parcel. Next time you use it, try two things. Before you send the prompt, think about how much information the chat really needs. When you get the answer, take a moment to check the detail that matters most.

The same habit helps when the decisions are bigger. A school, a business or a public office can ask where AI would help them and who would be responsible for a decision made with its help. We know that the choice of data, the goal the system is given and what it can access all affect what it can do and what mistakes it might make.
There’s one question to take with you beyond this book. Which decisions do you want to hand over to a tool, and which ones do you want to make using your own judgement?
